extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers and journalists covering Cold War/military/legal affairs
extracted.subtask_description: News reporting and documentation of POW repatriation/`explanation` sessions at Panmunjom and related military/legal procedural rules (armistice deadlines, custodial authority, observer rights, and state/federal testimony rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Armistice deadlines for POW explanations and release
rubrics_metrics.description: The armistice timetable: explanations to balking POWs must end by Dec. 23; prisoners refusing repatriation must be released to civilian status by Jan. 22 if the forthcoming Korean political conference has not decided their fate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article states the armistice terms specify explanations end Dec. 23 and release-to-civilian-status Jan. 22 if no political conference decision; applies even if a political conference is not held.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation-session (persuasion) procedure at Panmunjom
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardized procedure for an 'explanation' interview: Indian guards lead the prisoner into a tent, three Communist interviewers (the 'explainers') conduct the session, neutral NNRC representatives sit as observers, the prisoner may refuse to reply, then is left alone for a period (normally up to five minutes) to decide which of two doors to take (repatriation or stay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details and variations given: most interviews lasted less than two minutes; an Indian officer explained the prisoner 'need not reply to any questions unless he wanted to'; after the explainer speaks the prisoner is left alone 'not exceeding five minutes' (sometimes reduced to one minute if violent); observers/interpretation and seating arrangements (chair in center etc.) are described. The protocol includes repeating the instruction about which door to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of Indian custodial force to use force
rubrics_metrics.description: Indian custodial/guard forces are empowered to use force to rout prisoners out of their compounds and to move them to explanation booths when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reportedly Indian troops were 'empowered ... to use force if necessary'; commanders ordered extra troops; guards carried sticks and rifles and in incidents a battalion was pushed in to move prisoners. The article describes forcible measures (dragging, threats) when prisoners balked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observers' entitlement and dispute over access (Geneva Convention vs. NNRC/armistice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allied observers (U.N. Command) asserted entitlement under the Geneva Convention to watch operations in stockades, while NNRC/Indian chairman Thimayya overruled Allied requests citing armistice terms that allegedly do not allow Allied observers to visit compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brig. Gen. Hamblen insisted Allied observers were 'entitled to watch operations in the stockades under terms of the Geneva Convention'; Thimayya overruled requests on the ground armistice terms do not permit such visits — the article frames this as an operational/legal disagreement over observer access.

rubrics_metrics.name: NNRC/Communist right to recall prisoners for repeated questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: The Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission gives the Communist side broad opportunity to call prisoners back for repeated 'explanations' and questioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article notes the NNRC 'gives the Reds almost unlimited opportunity to call prisoners back for repeated questioning' and that this has scheduling/operational consequences (delays, repeated sessions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repatriation holding period for prisoners refusing to return
rubrics_metrics.description: Prisoners who refuse repatriation are to be held for a specified period (reported as 30 days) pending the outcome of political processes; if no decision is reached by the Jan. 22 deadline they are to be released to civilian status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article describes that those still refusing to go home 'will be held 30 days' and reiterates the Jan. 22 release/ civilian-status rule if the political conference has not settled their fate by then.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ohio state law protections for witnesses before legislative committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Ohio Common Pleas Judge ruling: the federal Fifth Amendment does not prohibit a state legislative committee from compelling testimony; Ohio law provides specific protections for witnesses testifying before legislative committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Bryant's summary of Ohio law: (1) testimony before a legislative committee may not be used in a criminal case against that witness; (2) the witness may not be prosecuted for any matter or thing concerning which he testifies before a legislative committee; (3) the witness may not be penalized for any transaction, matter or thing concerning which he testifies before a legislative committee. He emphasized these protections do not apply outside legislative investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential/agency policy on firing government workers who invoke the Fifth
rubrics_metrics.description: President Eisenhower made it a firing offense for any government worker to balk a Congressional committee by invoking the Fifth Amendment, giving agency heads discretion to fire employees who refuse to answer questions about Communist activity on grounds of self-incrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article frames the effect as providing 'agency heads discretion to fire any employee who refuses to answer questions about Communist activity on the grounds of possible self-incrimination.' This is reported as a policy change affecting employment consequences for invoking constitutional rights in congressional investigations.
